name: Dental midline correction

image.caption: Upper component of the modified twin block appliance with a midline screw

lead: The dental midline is the line between the upper or lower central incisors. Correction usually means orthodontic treatment so the midline lines up with the middle of the face and with the opposing arch, giving a straighter, more balanced smile.

Each arch has its own midline, and when the lower teeth shift sideways relative to the upper the midline is considered deviated; one reference example is a shift of about 2 mm. Orthodontic tooth movement shifts the arches so the midlines coincide. In looksmaxxing discussion, midline alignment is treated as one component of smile and facial symmetry. Reviewed sources describe the concept but give no clinical data on methods or on its effect on perceived attractiveness.

paras: People see an orthodontist, who assesses the midlines against the face and bite and plans tooth movement with braces or aligners. Duration depends on the case.
Details of risks were not covered by the sources reviewed; as with orthodontics in general, treatment is planned and monitored by a clinician.

web.title: The Impact of Midline Deviation on Smile Attractiveness (Cureus, 2025)

angle.text: Orthodontic realignment brings the line between the central incisors in line with the middle of the face, for a more symmetrical, balanced smile. The midline concept is clearly defined, and its effect on perceived appearance has not been measured in the sources reviewed.

lead: Dental midline correction is the adjustment of teeth, usually through orthodontic treatment, so that the line between the upper (or lower) central incisors lines up with the midline of the face or with the opposing arch. People pursue it for a more symmetrical, balanced smile: when the dental midline sits off-centre, the smile can look slightly skewed, and bringing it back to centre is one of the ways orthodontists tidy up the front of the smile. [1][2]

Each arch has its own midline, marking the contact between the central incisors. When the lower teeth shift sideways relative to the upper, the midline is described as deviated, for example a lower shift of about 2 mm to the left. [1] Case reports describe correcting midlines with differentiated orthodontic mechanics and with skeletal anchorage from mini-implants. [3][4]

Studies of how people perceive midline deviations suggest small shifts often pass unnoticed; a 2025 survey of 242 laypeople found shifts up to 3 mm were rated acceptable and attractive. [5] In looksmaxxing discussions, midline alignment is treated as one component of smile and facial symmetry.
infobox: Midsagittal line of the dental arches [1]
Lower teeth shifted about 2 mm to one side [1]
Braces with elastics, mini-implant anchorage, surgery in complex cases [3][4][6]
Braces usually one to three years [6]
Laypeople rated shifts up to 3 mm acceptable (one 2025 survey) [5]

paras: The dental midline refers to the contact point between the central incisors in each arch. In the textbook ideal, with teeth of ideal size, shape and position in maximum intercuspation, it is the midsagittal line of both arches. A deviation exists when the midlines of the upper and lower arches do not coincide. [1]

Orthodontic treatment uses fixed braces with wires that control tooth movement in three dimensions, and rubber elastics and springs that apply additional force; removable clear aligners are an alternative. [6] Braces typically stay on for one to three years, with adjustments every four to ten weeks, followed by retainer wear because teeth can relapse. [6]

Case reports describe more specialised approaches. A 2001 report described differentiated orthodontic mechanics for midline correction. [2] A 2009 case report used a two-component mini-implant for skeletal anchorage, noting that conventional tooth-borne mechanics for asymmetry can have side effects. [4] A 2014 case report in a cleft palate patient combined alveolar distraction with midline correction. [3] Severe malocclusions can require jaw surgery. [6]

A 2025 cross-sectional survey in Nablus asked 242 laypersons to rate smile attractiveness for upper midline deviations of 0 to 5 mm, shown as lips-only photographs and as photographs including the chin and part of the nose. Deviations up to 3 mm were rated acceptable and attractive in both sets, ratings declined at 4 and 5 mm, and adding the chin and nose did not significantly change ratings. [5]

The authors place their finding between earlier studies, which reported that shifts above 2 mm were unacceptable and that shifts up to 4 mm might go unnoticed. [5] A single small survey does not settle where the threshold lies for any given face.
Published work consists mainly of case reports of midline correction methods [2][3][4] and perception surveys. [5] No randomized trial of midline correction for appearance was located.
